claim: Maintenance of connective tissue integrity requires protein turnover to repair damaged tissue.
source: Maintenance of connective tissue integrity is fundamental to sustain function, requiring protein turnover to repair damaged tissue.
evidence: This is stated as a fundamental principle in the abstract and introduction, drawing on established scientific understanding.

claim: Connective tissue proteome dynamics remain largely undefined.
source: However, connective tissue proteome dynamics remain largely undefined, as do differences in turnover rates of individual proteins in the collagen and glycoprotein phases of connective tissue extracellular matrix (ECM).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Differences in turnover rates of individual proteins in the collagen and glycoprotein phases of connective tissue ECM remain undefined.
source: However, connective tissue proteome dynamics remain largely undefined, as do differences in turnover rates of individual proteins in the collagen and glycoprotein phases of connective tissue extracellular matrix (ECM).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Tendon has spatially distinct fascicular (collagen-rich) and interfascicular (glycoprotein-rich) ECM phases.
source: Here, we investigate proteome dynamics in the collagen and glycoprotein phases of connective tissues by exploiting the spatially distinct fascicular (collagen-rich) and interfascicular (glycoprotein-rich) ECM phases of tendon.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: There are approximately 1000-fold differences in protein turnover rates in tendon.
source: Our results demonstrate complex proteome dynamics in tendon, with ~1000 fold differences in protein turnover rates, and overall faster protein turnover within the glycoprotein-rich interfascicular matrix compared to the collagen-rich fascicular matrix.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Protein turnover is overall faster within the glycoprotein-rich interfascicular matrix compared to the collagen-rich fascicular matrix.
source: Our results demonstrate complex proteome dynamics in tendon, with ~1000 fold differences in protein turnover rates, and overall faster protein turnover within the glycoprotein-rich interfascicular matrix compared to the collagen-rich fascicular matrix.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Connective tissues consist of fibrous proteins (predominantly collagen) embedded in a glycoprotein-rich matrix.
source: Connective tissues consist of fibrous proteins (predominantly collagen) embedded in a glycoprotein-rich matrix (Scott, 1983), and variation in the organisation of both phases give rise to tissues with distinct structural and mechanical properties (Culav et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Scott, 1983.

claim: Variation in the organisation of collagen and glycoprotein phases gives rise to tissues with distinct structural and mechanical properties.
source: Connective tissues consist of fibrous proteins (predominantly collagen) embedded in a glycoprotein-rich matrix (Scott, 1983), and variation in the organisation of both phases give rise to tissues with distinct structural and mechanical properties (Culav et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Culav et al., 1999.

claim: Research in skin, tendon and cartilage indicates a relatively long half-life of collagens.
source: Research in a variety of tissues including skin, tendon and cartilage indicates a relatively long half-life of collagens, with more rapid turnover of glycoproteins and other non-collagenous proteins (Thorpe et al., 2010; Maroudas et al., 1998; Sivan et al., 2006; Sivan et al., 2008; Verzijl et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Glycoproteins and other non-collagenous proteins have more rapid turnover than collagens in skin, tendon and cartilage.
source: Research in a variety of tissues including skin, tendon and cartilage indicates a relatively long half-life of collagens, with more rapid turnover of glycoproteins and other non-collagenous proteins (Thorpe et al., 2010; Maroudas et al., 1998; Sivan et al., 2006; Sivan et al., 2008; Verzijl et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Several studies have reported negligible turnover of collagen within an individual's lifetime.
source: Indeed, several studies have reported negligible turnover of collagen, the major component of tendon and other connective tissues, within an individual's lifetime (Thorpe et al., 2010; Heinemeier et al., 2013; Heinemeier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thorpe et al., 2010; Heinemeier et al., 2013; Heinemeier et al., 2016.

claim: Other studies have measured relatively rapid collagen synthesis in tendon at basal levels and in response to exercise.
source: However other studies have measured relatively rapid collagen synthesis in tendon, both at basal levels and in response to exercise (Miller et al., 2005), and also identified soluble collagen with a much shorter half-life compared to the majority of collagen in human articular cartilage (Hsueh et al., 2019); the location(s) of these more labile proteins remain to be identified.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Miller et al., 2005.

claim: Soluble collagen with a much shorter half-life compared to the majority of collagen has been identified in human articular cartilage.
source: However other studies have measured relatively rapid collagen synthesis in tendon, both at basal levels and in response to exercise (Miller et al., 2005), and also identified soluble collagen with a much shorter half-life compared to the majority of collagen in human articular cartilage (Hsueh et al., 2019); the location(s) of these more labile proteins remain to be identified.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hsueh et al., 2019.

claim: The location(s) of more labile collagen proteins remain to be identified.
source: However other studies have measured relatively rapid collagen synthesis in tendon, both at basal levels and in response to exercise (Miller et al., 2005), and also identified soluble collagen with a much shorter half-life compared to the majority of collagen in human articular cartilage (Hsueh et al., 2019); the location(s) of these more labile proteins remain to be identified.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The glycoprotein-rich phase may be replenished more rapidly than the collagen-rich phase.
source: When taken together, these contradictory findings indicate that proteome dynamics in connective tissues is complex, and that the glycoprotein-rich phase may be replenished more rapidly than the collagen-rich phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the contradictory findings in the literature.

claim: The turnover rate of individual proteins within the different phases of the ECM remains undefined.
source: However, the turnover rate of individual proteins within the different phases of the extracellular matrix (ECM), and the potential contribution of differential regulation of protein turnover to maintenance of tissue homeostasis remain undefined.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The potential contribution of differential regulation of protein turnover to maintenance of tissue homeostasis remains undefined.
source: However, the turnover rate of individual proteins within the different phases of the extracellular matrix (ECM), and the potential contribution of differential regulation of protein turnover to maintenance of tissue homeostasis remain undefined.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Tendon consists of highly aligned, collagen-rich fascicular matrix (FM), interspersed by a less dense glycoprotein-rich phase termed the interfascicular matrix (IFM).
source: Tendon provides an ideal model in which to separately interrogate protein turnover in these ECM phases, as it consists of highly aligned, collagen-rich fascicular matrix (FM), interspersed by a less dense glycoprotein-rich phase, termed the interfascicular matrix (IFM, also referred to as the endotenon) (Kastelic et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kastelic et al., 1978.

claim: The FM is predominantly composed of type I collagen.
source: While the FM is predominantly composed of type I collagen, glycoproteins are also present in this region at low abundance (Thorpe et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Thorpe et al., 2016b.

claim: Glycoproteins are present in the FM at low abundance.
source: While the FM is predominantly composed of type I collagen, glycoproteins are also present in this region at low abundance (Thorpe et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Thorpe et al., 2016b.

claim: The IFM contains small amounts of a variety of collagens.
source: Similarly, the IFM contains small amounts of a variety of collagens (Södersten et al., 2013; Thorpe et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Södersten et al., 2013 and Thorpe et al., 2016b.

claim: It is possible to separate FM and IFM for individual analysis using laser capture microdissection.
source: Due to the highly aligned structure of tendon tissue, it is possible to separate FM and IFM for individual analysis using laser capture microdissection (Thorpe et al., 2016b; Zamboulis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thorpe et al., 2016b and Zamboulis et al., 2018.

claim: There is greater expression of markers of ECM degradation within the IFM.
source: Indeed, these, and other studies, have shown greater expression of markers of ECM degradation, as well as increased neo-peptide levels, a proxy measure of protein turnover, within the IFM (Spiesz et al., 2015; Thorpe et al., 2015a; Thorpe et al., 2016b), suggesting this region is more prone to microdamage, likely due to the high shear environment that occurs due to interfascicular sliding (Thorpe et al., 2012; Thorpe et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Spiesz et al., 2015; Thorpe et al., 2015a; Thorpe et al., 2016b.

claim: There are increased neo-peptide levels within the IFM.
source: Indeed, these, and other studies, have shown greater expression of markers of ECM degradation, as well as increased neo-peptide levels, a proxy measure of protein turnover, within the IFM (Spiesz et al., 2015; Thorpe et al., 2015a; Thorpe et al., 2016b), suggesting this region is more prone to microdamage, likely due to the high shear environment that occurs due to interfascicular sliding (Thorpe et al., 2012; Thorpe et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Spiesz et al., 2015; Thorpe et al., 2015a; Thorpe et al., 2016b.

claim: The IFM is more prone to microdamage, likely due to the high shear environment that occurs due to interfascicular sliding.
source: Indeed, these, and other studies, have shown greater expression of markers of ECM degradation, as well as increased neo-peptide levels, a proxy measure of protein turnover, within the IFM (Spiesz et al., 2015; Thorpe et al., 2015a; Thorpe et al., 2016b), suggesting this region is more prone to microdamage, likely due to the high shear environment that occurs due to interfascicular sliding (Thorpe et al., 2012; Thorpe et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations to Thorpe et al., 2012; Thorpe et al., 2015b.

claim: There is greater turnover of ECM proteins localised to the IFM than within the FM to repair local microdamage and maintain tendon homeostasis.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that there is greater turnover of ECM proteins localised to the IFM than within the FM to repair local microdamage and maintain tendon homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings discussed in the introduction.

claim: Novel bioinformatics software developments, in combination with in vivo isotope labelling and mass spectrometry technologies, provide the capacity to determine the turnover rates of individual proteins within a sample.
source: However, novel bioinformatics software developments, in combination with in vivo isotope labelling, and mass spectrometry technologies, now provide the capacity to determine the turnover rates of individual proteins within a sample (Kim et al., 2012; Lam et al., 2014; Lau et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2012; Lam et al., 2014; Lau et al., 2016.

claim: 2H enrichment of serum occurred rapidly in rats labelled with deuterium, reaching a plateau of 5.6% by day 4.
source: In rats labelled with deuterium over a period of 127 days (Figure 1a), 2H enrichment of serum occurred rapidly and in a similar manner to that reported previously in rodents (Kim et al., 2012), reaching a plateau of 5.6% by day 4, and remained constant throughout the study (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and comparison to previous studies.

claim: 2H enrichment of serum remained constant throughout the 127-day study.
source: In rats labelled with deuterium over a period of 127 days (Figure 1a), 2H enrichment of serum occurred rapidly and in a similar manner to that reported previously in rodents (Kim et al., 2012), reaching a plateau of 5.6% by day 4, and remained constant throughout the study (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 190 proteins with ≥2 unique peptides were identified in whole tendon digests.
source: 190 proteins with ≥2 unique peptides were identified in whole tendon digests and protein interactions are shown in Figure 2.
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomic analysis.

claim: Of the 190 proteins identified in whole tendon, 72 were classified as ECM or ECM-related proteins.
source: Of these proteins, 72 were classified as ECM or ECM-related proteins by MatrisomeDB (Hynes and Naba, 2012).
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomic analysis and classification.

claim: 266 proteins with ≥2 unique peptides were identified in the IFM.
source: In samples collected by laser capture microdissection of tendon cryosections, 266 proteins with ≥2 unique peptides were identified in the IFM, 79 of which were ECM or ECM-related proteins (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomic analysis.

claim: Of the 266 proteins identified in the IFM, 79 were ECM or ECM-related proteins.
source: In samples collected by laser capture microdissection of tendon cryosections, 266 proteins with ≥2 unique peptides were identified in the IFM, 79 of which were ECM or ECM-related proteins (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomic analysis and classification.

claim: 116 proteins with ≥2 unique peptides were identified in the FM.
source: In the FM, 116 proteins were identified, of which 71 were ECM or ECM-related proteins (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomic analysis.

claim: Of the 116 proteins identified in the FM, 71 were ECM or ECM-related proteins.
source: In the FM, 116 proteins were identified, of which 71 were ECM or ECM-related proteins (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomic analysis and classification.

claim: 455 peptides, relating to 41 proteins, passed the ProTurn selection criteria and were used to calculate protein half-life in whole tendon samples.
source: In total, 455 peptides, relating to 41 proteins, passed the ProTurn selection criteria and were used to calculate protein half-life in whole tendon samples.
evidence: This is a direct result from the data analysis.

claim: Decorin peptides demonstrate much faster turnover compared to collagen types 1 and 3.
source: Non-steady state curve fitting was performed by ProTurn to calculate turnover rate constants (k) for each peptide, and resultant fractional synthesis curves in Figure 5c&d demonstrate much faster turnover of decorin peptides compared to collagen types 1 and 3.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Collagenous proteins had the smallest k values, with corresponding half-lives of 330 to 1086 days.
source: As expected, the smallest k values related to collagenous proteins, with corresponding half-lives of 330 to 1086 days.
evidence: This is a direct result from the data analysis.

claim: Clusterin had the fastest turnover with a half-life of 1.4 days.
source: By contrast, the protein identified with the fastest turnover was the glycoprotein clusterin, with a half-life of 1.4 days.
evidence: This is a direct result from the data analysis.

claim: The half-life of proteoglycans ranged from 21 days for decorin to 72 days for lumican.
source: The half-life of proteoglycans ranged from 21 days for decorin to 72 days for lumican.
evidence: This is a direct result from the data analysis.

claim: With the exception of collagens, there was no clear relationship between protein class and rate of turnover.
source: With the exception of collagens, which all exhibited low turnover rates, there was no clear relationship between protein class and rate of turnover (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: 246 peptides, relating to 20 proteins, passed the ProTurn selection criteria in the FM.
source: 246 peptides, relating to 20 proteins, and 121 peptides, relating to 12 proteins, passed the ProTurn selection criteria in the FM and IFM respectively.
evidence: This is a direct result from the data analysis.

claim: 121 peptides, relating to 12 proteins, passed the ProTurn selection criteria in the IFM.
source: 246 peptides, relating to 20 proteins, and 121 peptides, relating to 12 proteins, passed the ProTurn selection criteria in the FM and IFM respectively.
evidence: This is a direct result from the data analysis.

claim: 55 peptides were present both in the IFM and FM.
source: 55 peptides were present both in the IFM and FM, and k values were significantly greater for these peptides in the IFM compared to the FM (median: 0.018 vs. 0.010; p<0.0001), demonstrating an overall faster rate of protein turnover in the IFM.
evidence: This is a direct result from the data analysis.

claim: k values were significantly greater for peptides present in both IFM and FM in the IFM compared to the FM (median: 0.018 vs. 0.010; p<0.0001).
source: 55 peptides were present both in the IFM and FM, and k values were significantly greater for these peptides in the IFM compared to the FM (median: 0.018 vs. 0.010; p<0.0001), demonstrating an overall faster rate of protein turnover in the IFM.
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: There is an overall faster rate of protein turnover in the IFM compared to the FM.
source: 55 peptides were present both in the IFM and FM, and k values were significantly greater for these peptides in the IFM compared to the FM (median: 0.018 vs. 0.010; p<0.0001), demonstrating an overall faster rate of protein turnover in the IFM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: 39 peptides relating to collagen type I were identified in both the IFM and FM.
source: 39 peptides relating to collagen type I were identified in both the IFM and FM, with significantly greater k values in the IFM (p<0.0001; Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a direct result from the data analysis.

claim: Collagen type I peptides had significantly greater k values in the IFM compared to the FM (p<0.0001).
source: 39 peptides relating to collagen type I were identified in both the IFM and FM, with significantly greater k values in the IFM (p<0.0001; Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Turnover rate constants for Col1a1 and Col1a2 were significantly higher in the IFM compared to the FM.
source: Turnover rate constants for Col1a1 and Col1a2 were significantly higher in the IFM compared to the FM, but there were no significant differences in rate constants for Col3a1 between tendon phases.
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: There were no significant differences in rate constants for Col3a1 between tendon phases.
source: Turnover rate constants for Col1a1 and Col1a2 were significantly higher in the IFM compared to the FM, but there were no significant differences in rate constants for Col3a1 between tendon phases.
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Rate constants of turnover of decorin peptides were significantly higher in the IFM compared to the FM (p=0.042).
source: Rate constants of turnover of decorin peptides were significantly higher in the IFM compared to the FM (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Protein turnover rate in tendon varied almost 1000-fold, with half-lives ranging from 1.5 days to over 1000 days.
source: Protein turnover rate in tendon varied almost 1000-fold, with half-lives ranging from 1.5 days to over 1000 days.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The results support the hypothesis that there is significantly faster turnover of proteins in the glycoprotein-rich IFM compared to the collagen-rich FM.
source: The results also support our hypothesis, demonstrating significantly faster turnover of proteins in the glycoprotein-rich IFM compared to the collagen-rich FM, both overall and when directly comparing individual proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The IFM had a more complex proteome than the FM, with a greater number of proteins identified in this region.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Thorpe et al., 2016b), the IFM had a more complex proteome than the FM, with a greater number of proteins identified in this region.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and comparison to previous studies.

claim: More proteins were identified within the IFM than in whole tendon samples.
source: Indeed, more proteins were identified within the IFM than in whole tendon samples; this is likely due to the predominance of collagen in whole tendon samples which precludes detection of proteins present at lower abundance in these samples.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data with an explanation.

claim: The predominance of collagen in whole tendon samples precludes detection of proteins present at lower abundance.
source: Indeed, more proteins were identified within the IFM than in whole tendon samples; this is likely due to the predominance of collagen in whole tendon samples which precludes detection of proteins present at lower abundance in these samples.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the observation.

claim: Collagen type I had a half-life from approximately 1.5 years in the IFM to 3 years in the FM.
source: Collagenous proteins had the slowest turnover of all tendon matrix proteins identified, in the whole tendon, and in the FM and IFM, with a half-life from approximately 1.5 years in the IFM to 3 years in the FM for type I collagen.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Collagen type III appeared to have a somewhat faster turnover rate than type I in both the FM and IFM.
source: Collagen type III appeared to have a somewhat faster turnover rate than type I in both the FM and IFM, with no significant difference between phases.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The IFM is enriched in collagen type III.
source: The IFM is known to be enriched in collagen type III, whereas the majority of collagen type I localises to the FM (Södersten et al., 2013; Thorpe et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Södersten et al., 2013 and Thorpe et al., 2016b.

claim: The majority of collagen type I localises to the FM.
source: The IFM is known to be enriched in collagen type III, whereas the majority of collagen type I localises to the FM (Södersten et al., 2013; Thorpe et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Södersten et al., 2013 and Thorpe et al., 2016b.

claim: Previous studies have reported that collagen is essentially inert in the adult rat patellar tendon.
source: While the collagen turnover rates measured are relatively slow, they contrast with previous studies which have reported that collagen is essentially inert in the adult rat patellar tendon (Bechshøft et al., 2017) and in tendons from larger animals (Heinemeier et al., 2013; Thorpe et al., 2010), as well as in cartilage and intervertebral disc (Heinemeier et al., 2016; Sivan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bechshøft et al., 2017.

claim: Previous studies have reported that collagen is essentially inert in tendons from larger animals.
source: While the collagen turnover rates measured are relatively slow, they contrast with previous studies which have reported that collagen is essentially inert in the adult rat patellar tendon (Bechshøft et al., 2017) and in tendons from larger animals (Heinemeier et al., 2013; Thorpe et al., 2010), as well as in cartilage and intervertebral disc (Heinemeier et al., 2016; Sivan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Heinemeier et al., 2013 and Thorpe et al., 2010.

claim: Previous studies have reported that collagen is essentially inert in cartilage and intervertebral disc.
source: While the collagen turnover rates measured are relatively slow, they contrast with previous studies which have reported that collagen is essentially inert in the adult rat patellar tendon (Bechshøft et al., 2017) and in tendons from larger animals (Heinemeier et al., 2013; Thorpe et al., 2010), as well as in cartilage and intervertebral disc (Heinemeier et al., 2016; Sivan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Heinemeier et al., 2016 and Sivan et al., 2008.

claim: Previous studies that measured collagen synthesis in human tendon using stable isotope labelling calculated a FSR of 0.04–0.06% hour−1, which equates to a half-life ranging from 48 to 64 days.
source: Other studies that have measured collagen synthesis in human tendon using stable isotope labelling and performing tendon biopsies, report contradictory findings, calculating a FSR of 0.04–0.06% hour−1, which equates to a half-life ranging from 48 to 64 days (Miller et al., 2005; Babraj et al., 2005; Smeets et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2005; Babraj et al., 2005; Smeets et al., 2019.

claim: Short term studies are likely to over-estimate FSR because not all newly synthesised protein would be incorporated into the matrix.
source: However, these were very short term studies, and it is unlikely that all newly synthesised protein would be incorporated into the matrix, such that FSR is over-estimated (Heinemeier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Heinemeier et al., 2013.

claim: The pool of more labile collagen identified previously in human tendon and cartilage may be located in the glycoprotein-rich ECM phase rather than with the bulk of the fascicular collagen.
source: The results we present here help to explain these apparent contradictory findings, suggesting that the pool of more labile collagen identified previously in human tendon and cartilage (Miller et al., 2005; Hsueh et al., 2019) may be located in the glycoprotein-rich ECM phase rather than with the bulk of the fascicular collagen.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the current findings and previous studies.

claim: Post-translational modifications are essential for determining protein structure and function.
source: Post-translational modifications are essential for determining protein structure and function, and are also likely to influence susceptibility to degradation by limiting enzyme access to cleavage sites (Jaisson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jaisson et al., 2007.

claim: Post-translational modifications are likely to influence susceptibility to degradation by limiting enzyme access to cleavage sites.
source: Post-translational modifications are essential for determining protein structure and function, and are also likely to influence susceptibility to degradation by limiting enzyme access to cleavage sites (Jaisson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jaisson et al., 2007.

claim: With ageing, partially degraded collagen accumulates within the equine superficial digital flexor tendon.
source: Indeed, a previous study has shown that, with ageing, partially degraded collagen accumulates within the equine superficial digital flexor tendon (Thorpe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Thorpe et al., 2010.

claim: Increased advanced glycation end products may render the ECM more resistant to degradation and subsequent remodelling, reducing the ability to repair damage within the tendon.
source: This is accompanied by increased advanced glycation end products which may render the ECM more resistant to degradation and subsequent remodelling, reducing the ability to repair damage within the tendon (Thorpe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to Thorpe et al., 2010.

claim: Overall protein turnover rate is likely more rapid in small compared to large animals.
source: In addition, it is likely that overall protein turnover rate is more rapid in small compared to large animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion.

claim: A recent study of protein turnover in dermal fibroblasts from different rodent species demonstrated a negative correlation between median k values and lifespan.
source: While few studies have directly compared protein turnover kinetics between species, a recent study of protein turnover in dermal fibroblasts from different rodent species demonstrated a negative correlation between median k values and lifespan (Swovick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Swovick et al., 2018.

claim: The half-life of serum albumin is approximately 10 fold greater in the human compared to the rat.
source: In support of this, the half-life of serum albumin is approximately 10 fold greater in the human compared to the rat (Chaudhury et al., 2003; Jeffay, 1960).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chaudhury et al., 2003 and Jeffay, 1960.

claim: Turnover of tendon ECM proteins is likely slower in larger animals than in the rat.
source: Taken together, it can be presumed that turnover of tendon ECM proteins is also likely slower in larger animals than those we report here for the rat, but the relative differences observed between individual proteins and ECM phases are likely to persist in humans and other large animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of species differences.

claim: The relative differences observed between individual proteins and ECM phases are likely to persist in humans and other large animals.
source: Taken together, it can be presumed that turnover of tendon ECM proteins is also likely slower in larger animals than those we report here for the rat, but the relative differences observed between individual proteins and ECM phases are likely to persist in humans and other large animals.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the discussion.

claim: Serum albumin and serotransferrin are predominantly synthesised and secreted by the liver.
source: Specifically, serum albumin and serotransferrin are predominantly synthesised and secreted by the liver (Tavill, 1972), whereas haemoglobin is synthesised in the bone marrow and its turnover provides a measure of erythrocyte lifespan (Koury, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tavill, 1972.

claim: Haemoglobin is synthesised in the bone marrow and its turnover provides a measure of erythrocyte lifespan.
source: Specifically, serum albumin and serotransferrin are predominantly synthesised and secreted by the liver (Tavill, 1972), whereas haemoglobin is synthesised in the bone marrow and its turnover provides a measure of erythrocyte lifespan (Koury, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koury, 2016.

claim: Anionic trypsin-1 is synthesised in the pancreas.
source: In addition, anionic trypsin-1, which had a particularly long half-life of nearly 2000 days in the FM, is synthesised in the pancreas.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Anionic trypsin-1 had a particularly long half-life of nearly 2000 days in the FM.
source: In addition, anionic trypsin-1, which had a particularly long half-life of nearly 2000 days in the FM, is synthesised in the pancreas.
evidence: This is a direct result from the data analysis.

claim: There may be a pool of trypsin within tendon that remains inactive until required for repair, which would explain the long half-life measured.
source: Proteases have a role in tissue repair (Shah and Mital, 2018); it is possible that there is a pool of trypsin within tendon that remains inactive until required for repair, which would explain the long half-life measured.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the observation, with a citation to Shah and Mital, 2018.

claim: GuHCl extraction has previously been shown to result in best proteome coverage for tendon.
source: We chose GuHCl extraction for whole tendon as this has previously been shown to result in best proteome coverage for tendon (Ashraf Kharaz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ashraf Kharaz et al., 2017.

claim: Protein half-lives were similar in the whole tendon and the fascicular matrix, suggesting minimal effects from using different extraction techniques.
source: Despite differences in extraction techniques used, protein half-lives were similar in the whole tendon and the fascicular matrix, suggesting minimal effects from using different extraction techniques.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: A previous study in which the rat Achilles was acid-solubilised post deuterium labelling reported a FSR of 0.66 % day−1 which equates to a half-life of 105 days.
source: Indeed, previous studies, in which the rat Achilles was acid-solubilised post deuterium labelling and FSR measured by GC-MS, reported a FSR of 0.66 % day−1 (Katsma et al., 2017) which equates to a half-life of 105 days, supporting the results we present here, in which average protein half-life in whole tendon is 131 days.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Katsma et al., 2017.

claim: Average protein half-life in whole tendon is 131 days.
source: Indeed, previous studies, in which the rat Achilles was acid-solubilised post deuterium labelling and FSR measured by GC-MS, reported a FSR of 0.66 % day−1 (Katsma et al., 2017) which equates to a half-life of 105 days, supporting the results we present here, in which average protein half-life in whole tendon is 131 days.
evidence: This is a direct result from the data analysis.

claim: The IFM has specialised composition and function, facilitating sliding between tendon fascicles to provide extensibility to the tendon.
source: Previous work has shown that the IFM has specialised composition and function, facilitating sliding between tendon fascicles to provide extensibility to the tendon (Thorpe et al., 2012; Thorpe et al., 2015b; Thorpe et al., 2016b; Thorpe et al., 2016c; Thorpe et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Cyclic sliding and recoil increases the risk of microdamage to the IFM.
